How much they resolve “depends on your guest requests, knowledge base, integrations, and escalation rules.” Source Haven already had Conduit installed at about 40 percent automation with listings uploaded, no workflows, and minimal knowledge-base work—so a live install is not readiness. Source Confirm whether a PMS path actually supplies live reservation context and whether messaging rides that connector. Opera Cloud is described as reservation and profile sync; it does not route guest messaging through that integration. Source Booking.com and VRBO were marked coming soon on the captured directory. Source A logo is not a supported action.

Timing versus later outcomes. Named situations to investigate, not needs every customer has: guest volume versus support seats (Haven, HomeHop, Canbnb); overnight voice (HomeHop 1–7 AM; independent-hotel after-hours copy); split inboxes or generic helpdesk misfit (Bocobay leaving Intercom); acquisition or multi-market expansion (Cascadia, Cosmica, Wynwood); owner support-cost / NOI (Lauderdale). Source Source “We cannot cover the next peak, night shift, or acquired portfolio” is buying timing. “We want 90% automation” or cap-rate math is a later adoption or outcome claim—do not use it as a qualification bar.

Qualification matrix

No weights. Unknown means investigate.

Criterion Dimension Positive observation Source / method Unknown or hold
Stay operator in FAQ industries Fit Hotel, serviced-apartment, or STR guest stays Site, OTA, PMS, discovery Hybrid RE+hospitality still in-category if stays are operated; exclude only non-stay businesses
Property-specific answers Fit Policies and booking context differ by property or listing Product claims + discovery Ask how answers differ by stay; generic ticket-only ops is a research flag
Channels Conduit unifies Readiness SMS, WhatsApp, email, calls, social, connected OTA threads Inbox FAQ vs their stack Source List required OTAs; hold if Booking.com/VRBO is mandatory until live status is confirmed
Reservation context path Readiness Connected PMS/OTA shows stay/booking beside the thread Integration page + demo Opera: messaging stays on existing hotel channels; confirm write-back separately
Knowledge + escalation owner Readiness Named person will standardize answers and review handoffs Ops interview (Haven pattern) Hold close until an owner exists; refusal to document policies is disqualifying for implementation
Present operating pressure Urgency Headcount lag, overnight gap, acquisition, call-center cost, two inboxes Jobs, news, discovery Hypothesis only—do not invent a timeline

Startup (0–25 units, $899/mo, no implementation fee) and per-unit starting rates ($18–$48) that “scale beyond 50 listings” are commercial bands, not ICP cutoffs. Source

Signals and sourcing

Search for operators and stacks, not buzzwords.

Signal Where to source What it tests Do not infer
Listings + PMS names (Guesty, Hostaway, Opera, Mews, Cloudbeds, Airbnb) Website, OTA, careers, integrations Fit and connector research Any write action; Airbnb card claims two-way messages and reservation modifications—verify for this account Source
Multi-channel guest lines Support pages, WhatsApp, phone Inbox / Agents path Full Suite operations jobs; nav still marks Operations coming soon
Guest-support or night hiring Job boards Timing hypothesis Headcount as a fit score
Acquisition, new market, OM/exit language Press Cascadia / Lauderdale / Bali-type situations Those customers’ dollar or automation results
Intercom / VoIP / prior AI failure Stack tools, reviews Bocobay / HomeHop / Flex-type misfit A guaranteed migration outcome

Company “300+ hospitality brands in 120+ countries” is reach copy, not named-account proof. Source

Discovery conversation

Collect observations that fill the matrix. Do not quote attributed rates as typical.

Draft questions:

  1. Who operates the stays, and is the contract with the owner, manager, or brand?
  2. Which channels must sit in one workspace on day one?
  3. Which system is source of truth for reservations, and should guest messaging stay on the PMS or move?
  4. Who owns property policies, and who reviews agent handoffs?
  5. What breaks if you add listings, an overnight window, or an acquired portfolio without new support seats? Haven reported adding 14 listings in January without adding support staff—ask whether that pressure exists; do not promise the result. Source
  6. Is the job unified inbox and voice (Messaging starting $18/unit/mo), portals/waivers/payments (Guest starting $30), devices, or Full Suite operational features? Operator is the workspace assistant; Operations is a separate coming-soon product label. Confirm the exact operational feature before quoting a delivery commitment. Source

Separate current pain (unread backlog, hour-long replies, two inboxes, Slack as the night desk) from later desired state (automation share, NOI, 24/7 autopilot).

Decision and handoff

Decision When observed Dependencies Handoff
Proceed In-category stays + connectable path + named knowledge/escalation owner. Timing evidence prioritizes the conversation; it is not a required fit gate Package choice after fit; write actions confirmed for this PMS Solution design with one named analog from customer-evidence, never an averaged rate
Research Lodging-adjacent; hotel group or serviced apartment without a story analog; OTA/PMS path unclear; Booking.com/VRBO required; unit vs listing undefined Integration owner + sales mapping Do not reject; log unknowns
Hold No guest-stay operation; no one will document policies; asked job is a physical check-in kiosk Hotel-groups copy: communication support, not a kiosk Source Polite close or recast the job

Packet: segment, stack versus live connectors, observed timing (not inferred attitude), open unknowns, and the entry product (Inbox/Agents versus Portals versus Workflows).

documents.title: Buyer problems & desired results
documents.summary: Hospitality buyers need guests answered, arrival-ready, and extras offered without growing a 24/7 communications desk as fast as the portfolio. Named KPIs in Conduit stories are desired measures and company-attributed outcomes, not typical rates or promised results.
documents.markdown:
## What this document means

This brief is about the work a hospitality buyer still has to get done and the result they would count as success. It is not a second catalog of [AI Agents](#knowledge/product-agents), [Inbox](#knowledge/product-inbox), [Guest Portals](#knowledge/product-portals), or [Workflows](#knowledge/product-workflows). Those surfaces can sit inside a job; they are not the job.

A desired KPI (share of conversations closed without a person, minutes to reply, support FTE, ancillary revenue, NOI) is what an operator would watch. It is not a promised result for the next account. Named figures below are Conduit-attributed stories collected in [Customer evidence & usable proof](#knowledge/customer-evidence). Use one named customer per motion; do not average rates. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/haven-2026)

Public FAQ copy says Conduit is for hotel teams, serviced-apartment operators, and short-term rental managers, with agents that answer messages and calls, handle routine requests, and coordinate with the team. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/industry/independent-hotels)

## Work buyers need to accomplish

The recurring job is: keep every guest conversation answered with the right property and booking context, complete the stay (access, payments, extras), and grow units or nights without a matching night desk.

| Job | Situation | Workaround | Failure | Capability in the job | Change they would measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cover threads without a night desk | After-hours calls, lockouts, late check-in | Call center, Google Voice, VA shifts | Hour waits; owner still in Slack | Agents on connected voice/chat/email/WhatsApp/OTA paths with available reservation context; confirm channel routing and supported actions per connector; escalate with history | First-response time; overnight hours covered; human issues per incident |
| One workspace for OTA + messaging + calls | Multi-channel STR or hotel | Two inboxes (e.g. Intercom + Hostaway) plus WhatsApp | Lost context; no performance view | Inbox with booking details beside the thread | Channels unified; time spent switching tools |
| Add units without linear guest-support hiring | 40→100+ listings or an acquisition | Hire per shift as volume climbs | Backlogs (e.g. 630 unread); model does not scale | Agents + workflows + knowledge teaching | Automation %; properties per support rep; hires avoided |
| Get guests arrival-ready without another app | Codes, deposits, waivers, extras | Email sequences, PDF guides, extra payment links | Guests still ask; access delayed | Portal: one branded stay link | Pre-arrival completion; inbound “how do I get in” volume |
| Offer extras in the live conversation | Unused rooms, gap nights, early check-in, spa | Pre-arrival upgrade emails | Independent-hotel page says those emails convert below 10% | Workflows/agents using booking rules | Ancillary attach—not a guaranteed lift |

[Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/agents) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/inbox) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/portals) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/workflows) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/industry/independent-hotels)

Agents answer using property information and reservation data, can create a task or update a booking through connected tools, and pass requests to the team. Inbox covers SMS, WhatsApp, email, calls, social, and connected OTA threads. Workflows send confirmations, check-in, follow-ups, and add-on offers the operator chooses. Portals give one stay link (no app) for details, checks, pay, upgrades, and the AI concierge. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/agents.md) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/inbox.md) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/workflows.md) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/portals.md)

Segment flavor, not extra jobs: independent hotels want after-hours cover while the desk serves people in the lobby; hotel groups want shared brand standards with per-property policies; short-term rentals want listing-specific check-in and booking-change handling. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/industry/independent-hotels) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/industry/hotel-groups) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/industry/short-term-rentals)

## Before and after workflows

**Scenario 1 — STR growth is a staffing problem.** Haven Vacation Rentals managed roughly 270 Smoky Mountain listings. Peak guest support was about 25 people across shifts. Conduit was already installed near 40% automation with few workflows; volume still scaled with units. After the team standardized answers and taught the system, the 2026 write-up reports 90% automation, two people per shift, 14 January listings without extra support hires, and scores held around 4.8–4.9. In a snowstorm with 90 same-day check-ins, three issues needed a human. That is Haven’s attributed path, not a template rate. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/haven-2026)

HomeHop’s same job after a failed AI vendor and a Google Voice lockout: roughly 40 to 108 listings without extra guest-support hires, 70% automation, and voice coverage 1 AM–7 AM. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/homehop)

**Scenario 2 — Boutique hotel as a hands-off asset.** The Lauderdale Boutique Hotel had cycled through Jurny’s PMS/call center and other hospitality call services: costs from $4,000 down to $1,200 a month, guests waiting up to an hour, the owner still answering Slack, refunds mounting. Desired result was investor-grade, low-touch operations. The story reports support at $600/month, average response 57 minutes to 2 minutes, NOI up at least $3,400/month from costs and fewer refunds, and an 8% cap-rate translation of that NOI into more than $500,000 of modeled asset value. The write-up describes an AI platform plus a 24/7 staffed support team, so the software-only contribution is not isolated. Cap-rate math is the owner’s model, not an appraisal. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/lauderdale-hotel)

**Separate STR acquisition example — Cascadia Getaways.** The vacation-rental manager reports 60% automation and a 4.9 communication score across 100 properties. During acquisition integration, leadership expressed confidence about adding properties without extra guest-service hires; this is an expectation, not a completed staffing result or hotel proof. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/cascadia-getaways)

## How improvement would be measured

Pair each desired change with a source of truth. Do not treat a story number as an SLA.

| Desired change | Named, attributed examples | Not the same as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work closed without a person | Haven 40%→90%; HomeHop 70%; Canbnb 60% of ~1,500 msgs/week; Flex title 70% vs header 90% | A comparable denominator or product guarantee |
| Speed | Lauderdale 57 min→2 min avg; Wynwood resolution 14–15 min→3 min | Instant replies on every issue |
| Staffing / cost | Haven ~25→two per shift (page: no AI layoffs); Easy BnB ~$22k/month and 11 VAs replaced, reported on the Bali Luxury Stays page | The same layoff vs. no-layoff outcome everywhere |
| Quality while automating | Haven 4.8–4.9; Cascadia locked at 4.9 | Proof that reviews always rise |
| Revenue / asset | Cosmica ~5% of Dubai revenue from upsells/cross-sells at peak; Lauderdale NOI/cap math | Typical ancillary % |

[Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/haven-2026) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/homehop) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/canbnb) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/the-flex) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/lauderdale-hotel) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/wynwood-house) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/bali-luxury-stays) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/cosmica) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/cascadia-getaways)

Conduit’s agent FAQ says how much agents resolve depends on guest requests, knowledge base, integrations, and escalation rules, and to track resolved conversations and handoffs. Inbox FAQ says messaging automation depends on the requests and how agents are configured. Those are measurement instructions, not forecasts. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/agents.md) [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/inbox.md)

## Turning problems into campaigns

Lead with the job, then one named proof, then the surface. Drafts must not invent a relationship or claim every customer shares the pain. Writing rules: [Campaign writing examples & rules](#knowledge/writing-examples), [Audience-to-message map](#knowledge/message-map).

- **Cannot hire as fast as units.** Haven or HomeHop; ask current automation %, overnight headcount, and whether policies live in one knowledge base. [ICP · vacation-rental operators](#knowledge/icp-rentals).
- **Guests wait; owner still in Slack.** Lauderdale minutes and support cost; confirm call-center spend and refund leakage. [ICP · hotel operators](#knowledge/icp-hotels).
- **Two inboxes.** Bocobay left Intercom to unify WhatsApp, email, phone, and live chat. The page header “80% resolution” / “100s hours” is not derived in the body—do not lead with it. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/customers/bocobay)
- **After hours is the real desk.** Independent-hotel after-hours language plus HomeHop 1–7 AM voice. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/industry/independent-hotels)
- **Money left on extras.** Workflows can offer early check-in, gap nights, and upgrades; Cosmica’s ~5% Dubai figure is one market’s peak. [Source](https://www.conduit.ai/product/workflows.md)

This pack has no hotel-group P&L body, no isolated Portals outcome, and no shared automation denominator. Investigate those before writing group-wide guarantees. Capability mapping: [Product catalog & capability map](#knowledge/products-capabilities).

Which named hotel-group or multi-property hotel outcomes exist beyond Lauderdale and Wynwood, which is multi-market CX rather than group ops?
Do any named stories isolate Guest Portals (pre-arrival completion, deposits, in-portal upgrades) as the cause of a result?

documents.title: Visual identity & logo pack
documents.markdown:
This identity guide separates original company files, observed website presentation and provider candidates. It gives a designer usable source assets while keeping incomplete parts of the logo family visible.

## Logo family and background fit

| Placement | Available asset | Status and use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wordmark on light | Dark, transparent website SVG | Official original. Preserve aspect ratio and original lettering. |
| Wordmark on dark | Same website SVG with the footer’s white display treatment | Observed website usage. This is a rendering treatment, not a separately downloaded white master. |
| Icon on dark | Pale, transparent 512px website PNG | Official original; prefer this over the smaller provider version. |
| Icon on light | Dark icon in a 100px provider JPEG tile | Incomplete for transparent high-resolution placement. Request an official dark master. |

The website’s Apple touch icon and site icon are opaque square tiles. They are useful app identity references, but they must not replace the transparent assets in an ad lockup. The Brandfetch pale PNG uses palette transparency; the earlier analysis incorrectly described the viewer background as part of the image. File inspection corrected that error. [Website](https://www.conduit.ai/)

## Color and typography

The live website uses white as the main canvas, #29251E for body text, and #28241E for its dark primary buttons. Brandfetch also supplied #F3F1EC and #77D4FF; retain those as provider palette candidates rather than inventing a complete set of semantic UI tokens. A color being present does not establish its correct use for errors, focus rings or every campaign background.

The website CSS identifies Neue Montreal for body typography and Season Mix for the display face. It also declares fallbacks and other fonts. A fallback declaration is not evidence that Arial is Conduit’s primary brand font. Font files and licensing need to be handled by the existing platform ingestion pipeline before export. [Official stylesheet](https://www.conduit.ai/_next/static/chunks/171m6_plm0ner.css?dpl=dpl_5zNSTYuHzmG9DtT6CUng5Pms8gTY)

## How an agent should use this pack

Choose a slot by background contrast and use the original asset identity. For one-to-one ads, compose the seller and target-company marks as separate image layers; do not ask an image model to draw either logo. Preserve proportions, align optical height and allow deliberate space around the separator. The exact clear-space rule is not published in these captured sources and needs brand confirmation.

Website treatments may be reproduced only as explicitly recorded presentation instructions. Do not silently produce new logo files or declare missing variants approved. The standalone preview shows the observed reverse-wordmark treatment so a human can inspect it; the original SVG remains unchanged.

## Remaining gaps and next action

The four intended slots are now visible, but the pack is not four approved transparent masters. The light-background icon still needs an official transparent dark file. If server export cannot preserve the footer treatment, request a reverse wordmark master as well. Confirm spacing, palette roles and font permissions before campaign approval. Brand ingestion should keep these availability states separate from a successful provider HTTP response.

The website’s Apple touch icon and site icon are opaque square tiles. They are useful app identity references, but they must not replace the transparent assets in an ad lockup. The Brandfetch pale PNG uses palette transparency; the earlier analysis incorrectly described the viewer background as part of the image. File inspection corrected that error. Website

Color and typography

The live website uses white as the main canvas, #29251E for body text, and #28241E for its dark primary buttons. Brandfetch also supplied #F3F1EC and #77D4FF; retain those as provider palette candidates rather than inventing a complete set of semantic UI tokens. A color being present does not establish its correct use for errors, focus rings or every campaign background.

The website CSS identifies Neue Montreal for body typography and Season Mix for the display face. It also declares fallbacks and other fonts. A fallback declaration is not evidence that Arial is Conduit’s primary brand font. Font files and licensing need to be handled by the existing platform ingestion pipeline before export. Official stylesheet

How an agent should use this pack

Choose a slot by background contrast and use the original asset identity. For one-to-one ads, compose the seller and target-company marks as separate image layers; do not ask an image model to draw either logo. Preserve proportions, align optical height and allow deliberate space around the separator. The exact clear-space rule is not published in these captured sources and needs brand confirmation.

Website treatments may be reproduced only as explicitly recorded presentation instructions. Do not silently produce new logo files or declare missing variants approved. The standalone preview shows the observed reverse-wordmark treatment so a human can inspect it; the original SVG remains unchanged.

Remaining gaps and next action

The four intended slots are now visible, but the pack is not four approved transparent masters. The light-background icon still needs an official transparent dark file. If server export cannot preserve the footer treatment, request a reverse wordmark master as well. Confirm spacing, palette roles and font permissions before campaign approval. Brand ingestion should keep these availability states separate from a successful provider HTTP response.

documents.title: Library organization & research flow
documents.markdown:
This library organizes one company's public evidence into documents that support specific sales and campaign decisions. The folder name tells a reader where to look; each document also carries a stable internal identifier, source references and dependencies for an agent. The same evidence can support several decisions without creating several conflicting versions of the fact.

## What belongs in each folder

| Folder | Documents and ownership | Use it to answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Company | Company overview; commercial model and market context | What business is this, how does it earn revenue, and which market does it serve? |
| Product | Catalog, individual product guides, Operator availability, developer capabilities, integrations and pricing | Which specific capability addresses the problem, and what are its limits and prerequisites? |
| Brand & messaging | Positioning, voice, message map and proposed writing examples | What should we say, why does it matter, and how should it sound? |
| Audience | ICP strategy, hotel and rental profiles, buying committee, qualification and buyer problems | Which account is worth pursuing, who matters, what evidence is missing, and what question comes next? |
| Proof | Customer evidence and alternatives | What supports the argument, and how narrowly may we use a result or comparison? |
| Design | Identity pack and usage guide | Which original logo or asset fits this surface, and what is its source? |

Assets has its own unified library: website images, product visuals, customer logos and LinkedIn ads. Ads are a source filter inside Assets, not a separate knowledge folder. A product page is a knowledge source; a screenshot from that page is an asset; the asset links back to the relevant product guide.

## Why there are multiple product documents

The catalog explains the product system. The AI Agents, Inbox, Guest Portals and Workflows guides each explain a different buying decision: purpose, users and buyers, capabilities, limitations, workflows, integration dependencies, pricing/package fit, differentiation, evidence and discovery questions. Operator and developer capabilities have their own guides because an internal assistant, an API and a marketed product are not interchangeable.

Pricing is owned by one rate-card document. Product guides can cite its package context, but cannot invent a standalone product price. Proof owns named customer outcomes. Audience documents use those cases to propose a fit hypothesis; they cannot turn a case's unit count or savings into a universal qualification rule. Brand voice owns inferred writing guidance, not new product facts.

## What triggers each step

| Trigger | Research action | Output and dependency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A company website is supplied | Resolve company/domain; inspect homepage, about, product navigation and original brand assets | Initial company identity and visible asset candidates; rich research continues in the background |
| A distinct product is found | Read its official page, relevant documentation, integration/setup pages and applicable case studies | A dedicated product guide; catalog updated without treating every SEO use-case page as a product |
| Company and product evidence is available | Compare official positioning and language with named customer situations | Positioning, voice and message map; all remain proposed guidance |
| Product, integration, price and customer evidence is complete enough | Build account fit and buyer-role hypotheses; identify commercial unknowns | ICP strategy, segment profiles and qualification decisions |
| An original image or ad is acquired | Retain original bytes and source identity; inspect content and composition | Human description and structured Agent context in Assets |
| A source changes or a user corrects a document | Revisit the owning fact and its dependants | A new revision; earlier drafts and human decisions must remain recoverable |

In this rework, company/product/proof writing runs in bounded parallel jobs. Messaging waits for its product and proof dependencies; audience writing follows, and the qualification playbook waits for the ICP strategy. Exact source passages and source links are checked before a draft enters the viewer. These structural checks do not prove that every inference is correct; semantic review remains a separate step.

## What an agent receives

Human documents use headings, prose and tables. Their structured record adds the document's purpose, decisions supported, source IDs, dependencies, unresolved questions and proposed qualification criteria. Selecting an asset exposes a concise description first. **Agent context** adds observed visual content, interpreted use, composition/crop guidance, related product documents, audience hypotheses, restrictions, source identity and original file hash. A badge means context exists, not that the image or claim has been approved for a campaign.

“Buyer problems & desired results” is the plain-language name for jobs and outcomes: what work the buyer needs to accomplish, what fails in the present approach, and what improvement they would measure. It is the bridge from product capability to a relevant sales argument.

## How this maps to Clue today

The platform audit was read-only. Existing knowledge records already carry path, title, kind, version, status, product or ICP identity, Markdown, front matter and source references. Current knowledge folders are Company, Product, Audience and Proof. Design is owned by the brand kit. The additional Brand & messaging folder is an experiment proposal and would require an explicit future contract change.

The current brand kit has logo variants with asset identity, color mode and dimensions; logos and images also have title, description and usage notes. The frontend mapper currently chooses description **or** usage note for its description field, so useful guidance can disappear from the visible card. A future contract should preserve both, add a versioned structured context record, and keep human approval distinct from analysis completion. No such platform change was made here.

The existing onboarding driver begins ICP synthesis after its company/catalog phase while deeper product research continues. The proposed improvement is a useful preliminary profile early, followed by an evidence-informed revision after the relevant product reports arrive. This experiment demonstrates that ordering; it does not deploy it.

## Review and maintenance

Public sources can contradict one another or omit commercial details. Missing evidence produces a specific question, not an invented revenue band, buyer title, logo variant or guaranteed result. Approval should resolve consequential policies such as target geography, minimum deal size, serviceability and campaign claim wording. After approval, an integration should use the platform's existing claim, artifact, tenancy and versioning seams. The standalone files are review artifacts, not a parallel production source of truth.

analysis.name: STR operator dashboard LinkedIn ad
analysis.description: Square published LinkedIn ad with Conduit wordmark, headline on AI agents for short-term rentals, and a white UI card screenshot of the Conduit operator dashboard answering a query on high-value bookings with three metric tiles.

observed.composition: White upper band holding left-aligned wordmark and large headline; lower green-to-lime gradient holding a centered white rounded product card with query bubble, analysis line, three stat tiles, and two footer links.
observed.colors: White field, black type, lime-to-forest green gradient, pale blue metric tiles, dark gray UI copy.
observed.text: conduit. AI agents that understand short-term rentals. Conduit operator. For all bookings over $1000 per night, how many questions did guests ask on average—and how fast did my team respond to the ones the AI escalated? Analyzed 38 bookings · 241 guest questions · 46 escalations. Guests asked 6.4 questions per booking. The AI resolved 81% without help. For escalated questions, your team's median first response was 4m 12s. QUESTIONS PER BOOKING 6.4 average. ESCALATED TO TEAM 19% of questions. TEAM RESPONSE TIME 4m 12s median. 12% faster than the previous 90 days. Compare RevPAR by property for the last 90 days. Show the escalated conversations.
observed.logo_placement: Black lowercase conduit wordmark, top-left on the white band.

guidance.use_when: Showing STR operators a concrete operator-dashboard view of AI-handled vs escalated guest questions.
guidance.how_to_use: Run the full 1200×1200 creative as a LinkedIn or similar square ad; keep headline + screenshot together so the query context remains readable.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not use if the live operator UI or the $1000-booking filter no longer matches; do not isolate tiles without the surrounding ad frame or wordmark.
guidance.crop_and_placement: Keep the entire composition. Never crop the conduit wordmark. The green band is not a reusable background asset.
guidance.background_suitability: Self-contained; the green gradient is part of the ad and should not be extracted for other layouts.

analysis.product_or_use_case: Operator analytics for AI guest-messaging in short-term rentals.
analysis.inferred_audience: Short-term rental operators and property managers reviewing AI impact on guest questions.
uncertainties: Whether the dashboard UI, 6.4 / 19% / 4m 12s figures, and RevPAR link still match the current product.

analysis.description: Square published LinkedIn ad with headline on autopilot guest messages and a product screenshot of the Insights view showing automation rate, guest satisfaction, a trend line, and channel volume bars.

observed.composition: White upper band with left wordmark, large headline and subhead; lower peach-to-pink gradient holding a white Insights card with two KPI tiles, a line chart, and four horizontal channel bars.
observed.colors: White, black type, peach-pink-orange gradient, green positive deltas, blue line and bars, light gray chart area.
observed.text: conduit. 3 out of every 5 guest messages, handled on autopilot. Let your team focus on the moments that truly need a human. Insights. Last 30 days. Automation rate 77.5% +6.2%. Guest satisfaction 96% +2.8%. Automation rate chart 73.0% to 77.5% Jun 22–Jul 20. Message volume SMS 4,980 34%, WhatsApp 4,320 29%, Email 3,180 22%, Voice AI 2,176 15%.
observed.logo_placement: Black lowercase conduit wordmark, top-left on white.

guidance.use_when: Illustrating channel mix and rising automation rate for hospitality teams evaluating AI guest messaging.
guidance.how_to_use: Use the complete square as social creative; the Insights card can be referenced only while the surrounding headline remains visible.
guidance.avoid_when: Avoid if current Insights UI, 77.5% figure, or channel split has changed; do not crop the wordmark or present the chart as live data.
guidance.crop_and_placement: Retain full 1200×1200. Do not crop logo or KPI tiles independently of the ad frame.
guidance.background_suitability: Gradient is baked into the ad; not a standalone background.

analysis.product_or_use_case: Insights dashboard for automation rate and multi-channel guest-message volume.
analysis.inferred_audience: Hospitality operators tracking how many guest messages AI handles versus human.
uncertainties: Currency of 77.5% / 96% KPIs, chart dates, and channel volume numbers versus live product.

analysis.name: Sarcastic one-star review ad
analysis.description: Square published LinkedIn ad styled as a one-star customer review complaining that the team now has nothing to do, closed by the line We'll take it.

observed.composition: Soft pastel blur background; top-left wordmark; centered white review card with avatar initials, 1.0-of-5 stars, headline and body copy, helpful-vote count; large We'll take it. below the card.
observed.colors: Peach-blue-yellow blur, white card, gold empty stars, black type.
observed.text: conduit. CUSTOMER REVIEW. Dale Brackett Owner at Coastal Beach Vacations · 240 listings. 1.0 out of 5. My team has nothing to do anymore. Since we turned on Conduit, the AI answers every guest message before anyone on my guest services team can get to it. They just play solitaire on their laptops all day now. One star. Reviewed 3 days ago. Was this helpful? 147. We'll take it.
observed.logo_placement: Black conduit wordmark top-left; no other logos.

guidance.use_when: Humorous social creative that reframes over-automation as a positive outcome for guest-services teams.
guidance.how_to_use: Keep the ironic one-star framing and closing line intact; do not present the review as a genuine 1-star rating of Conduit.
guidance.avoid_when: Avoid in contexts that require strictly positive testimonials or where sarcasm could be misread as a real complaint; do not crop the wordmark.
guidance.crop_and_placement: Full square only. Do not isolate the review card without We'll take it. or the conduit mark.
guidance.background_suitability: Blurred field belongs to this ad and is not a reusable background.

analysis.product_or_use_case: AI that answers guest messages before human staff, framed humorously.
analysis.inferred_audience: Hospitality operators who would appreciate a tongue-in-cheek take on full automation of guest messaging.
uncertainties: The review is clearly satirical; Coastal Beach Vacations and Dale Brackett may be illustrative rather than verified customers.

analysis.name: Competitors using AI phone-notes ad
analysis.description: Square published LinkedIn ad with left-side headline about competitors using AI and a right-side iPhone mockup showing a Notes list titled VRMA Notes that mentions Conduit.ai.

observed.composition: Soft purple-pink-orange gradient; left column with wordmark and two-line headline; right column a black-bezel iPhone displaying a Notes app with four bullets and bottom toolbar.
observed.colors: Lavender-to-peach gradient, white phone screen, black UI chrome, orange Conduit.ai link, black type.
observed.text: conduit. Your competitors are using AI. Are you? 11:11. VRMA Notes. Check out Conduit.ai — seems like everyone is using it. Start documenting my SOPs. Research what an “agentic workflow” actually is. On the Conduit demo, ask them how much money I’m leaving on the table by not upselling damage waivers.
observed.logo_placement: Black conduit wordmark top-left of the ad (outside the phone).

guidance.use_when: FOMO-style creative aimed at operators who attend industry events (VRMA) and may be evaluating Conduit.
guidance.how_to_use: Keep phone mockup and left headline together; the Notes list is illustrative copy, not a real user’s notes.
guidance.avoid_when: Do not treat the Notes bullets as customer quotes or as an official VRMA endorsement; do not crop the conduit wordmark.
guidance.crop_and_placement: Use full square. Do not crop the phone or the wordmark; the gradient is not a separate background asset.
guidance.background_suitability: Gradient is integral to this ad.

analysis.product_or_use_case: Competitive awareness for AI agents in vacation-rental operations, including upsell of damage waivers.
analysis.inferred_audience: Vacation-rental managers familiar with VRMA who have not yet adopted AI guest messaging.
uncertainties: VRMA Notes is staged copy inside a mockup, not evidence of VRMA partnership or real user notes.

We've officially connected Conduit to
Mews
. Your AI agent can now read what's in
Mews
and act on it, on its own.

For a while, an agent connected to your PMS could answer a question about a booking. Now it can do the work behind it.

With Mews connected, the agent can:

→ Pull the live reservation: dates, status, balance, access codes
→ Look up a guest, including VIP or blocklist status, and reply in their language
→ Move a check-in or check-out when a guest asks
→ Cancel a reservation, applying the fee per your policy
→ Open a housekeeping or maintenance task and route it to the right department
→ Drop an internal note on the reservation for the team

So when a guest says the AC is out, the agent opens a maintenance task for the right department, notes it on the reservation, and tells the guest it's handled. No one has to touch it.

Runs on Mews? Book a demo in the comments below.

Already on Conduit? Add Mews in Settings → Connections.

Three to try on the marketplace today:

Ad Details
Conduit
Promoted
Conduit now connects to OPERA Cloud by
Oracle
Hospitality, the property management system that runs a huge share of the world's hotels.

For a hotel, an AI agent is only as good as what it knows and what it can do. Connecting OPERA gives Conduit both.

What it knows:
Reservations, guest contact details, bookings, and listings sync into Conduit, along with live availability across every room type, including group blocks. The agent knows who's arriving, what they booked, which property's rules apply, and what's open to sell right now.

What it can do:
Through Conduit's MCP adapter for PMSes, the agent gets the full Oracle API, effectively a direct line into OPERA. It can create and modify reservations and handle the work a front desk does, on its own.

On the revenue side:
Because the agent sees live availability and can connect to your CRM, it works group sales too, running outreach to fill open blocks before they hit cutoff.

This isn't a chat assistant sitting inside your PMS. It's an agent that sees your live inventory and your guests, and can act on both.

We've had voice agents for a while. Now they've gotten a lot better.

For a long time, voice AI was good at conversation and not much else. It could answer questions and take a message, but anything that touched a real system ended with "let me have someone follow up."

What changed is real-time tool calling. The models have been smart enough to pick the right tool and use it in the middle of a live call, fast enough that the guest never feels a long pause. 

And with our hospitality MCPs, our voice agent can take a booking in your PMS, change a reservation, or reset a door code, on the call, without a handoff.

For our initial group of users, voice resolution went from 56% to 92%. That is the share of calls the agent finishes on its own, no callback, no human handoff.

AI agents that elevate the guest experience requires the work to be done while the guest is still on the line.

ad_detail_evidence.source_text:
Punn Kam

Promoted by Conduit

Guests in LatAm send 2x more messages than in North America.

We looked at millions of guest messages on Conduit and averaged them by property. The spread was not what I expected.

Messages per property per month:

- Latin America: 23.7
- Middle East and Africa: 21.5
- Europe: 19.0
- Asia-Pacific: 15.4
- North America: 10.3

Latin America runs more than double North America. Inside the regions it gets wider still, with Argentina at 52.5 and Brazil at 43.1 against Australia at 10.4 and the United States at 9.6.

I don't think there's a single cause. North America may be more established with self-check-ins, which reduce message volume. The density of Latin America might make navigation more confusing. 

Whatever the reason, operators must staff up for the demand across both the average and on seasonal peaks. AI agents must play a major role in that staffing plan.

Full analysis in the comments.

About the ad

Single Image Ad

Advertiser Conduit

Paid for by HostAI Labs, Inc.

Ran from Aug 7, 2026 to Sep 10, 2026

ad_detail_evidence.source_text:
Cole Rubin

Promoted by Conduit

Today we're launching Portals, the biggest release in Conduit's history.

Portals is one link for everything a guest needs. Check-in, upsells, payments, and a chat agent built in that answers their questions and books the upsells itself.

Here's the flow:

1. A guest books a stay and gets texted their portal link
2. They verify with a selfie against their ID
3. They sign the check-in waiver
4. Their room key drops into their wallet, and they land in their portal: custom upsell offers and every detail of the stay in one place

Then it's check-in day. They show up, walk to the room, and swipe to open. If the room is already cleaned, an early check-in offer pops up: get in now for $40. 

Land somewhere before 1pm and you're buying that every time. And it's easy money the hotel used to leave on the table.

If you're already on Conduit, it's live in your sidebar right now.

If you're not yet, change that by clicking the link in the comments to talk to our team. 

Btw, if these don't pay for themselves, you don't pay for it!

About the ad

Single Image Ad

Advertiser Conduit

Paid for by HostAI Labs, Inc.

Punn Kam

Promoted by Conduit

A boutique hotel upsold me before I ever set foot in the building.

24 hours before check-in, instead of the usual "Dear guest, your check-in instructions are attached" email, they texted me a link.

I opened it on my phone: directions from the airport, my room details, the wifi password. While I was poking around, an early check-in and a massage showed up on the front page, and I bought them with Apple Pay, all before I left for my flight.

Then, the moment I landed, I received another text: "Hi Punn, we have a discounted upgrade on the Corner King room you stayed in last time. Let me know if you'd like it. The offer's also in your portal." I thought about it for a second and went for the upgrade.

That hotel made more money off my stay before I walked in, and I had an incredible experience. Because it was so personalized and timely, it never felt like a pitch. It felt like a personal concierge at a hotel who already knew what I liked and exactly when to reach out.

There's demand buried in millions of guest conversations every day. Almost none of it gets captured, because until now it hasn't been practical to.

That's why we built Portals.

It's a single link for the entire stay: instructions, directions, wifi details, digital room keys, in-room controls, an agent that answers anything, and upsell offers personalized to every guest.

Your agents personalize each portal in the conversation and place the most relevant offers at the top. Guests pay in a double-tap with Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link, and more.

Portals is live in Conduit today. Really proud of the team for building a best-in-class product yet again.

ad_detail_evidence.source_text:
Cole Rubin

Promoted by Conduit

Francesco Taiano runs short-term rentals across Italy and Dubai. In one year, upsells alone reached 5% of his Dubai revenue. Here's how he did it:

Initially, his team was spending most of the day answering the same guest questions over and over, then re-answering them in a different language. 

On top of that, 50 to 70% of the maintenance issues guests reported were things they could've fixed themselves in two minutes, if someone had just walked them through it. 

To keep up with the volume, he was running virtual assistant teams out of the Philippines and Pakistan just to cover the messages, a workaround that kept things running but didn't let the business grow.

So he moved the whole operation onto Conduit and built custom tooling on top of it: 

- A smart-lock integration for guest check-in
- Automated payment links
- A knowledge base he manages himself

As a result:

→ Guests now get instant answers in their own language, and the agent walks them through minor maintenance fixes on the spot
→ Positive reviews went up over the year, because guests get help the moment they need it instead of waiting on a VA at 2am
→ The same internal team now covers both Italy and Dubai, freed up for sales and new business, with no new hires

Instead of shrinking his team, Francesco used AI to let them do more, and stopped needing outside help just to keep the lights on.

--

We wrote a breakdown of how Francesco built this out, including the custom tooling behind it and exactly how the upsell automation escalates offers straight to the provider.

commentary.text:
Every guidebook, welcome book and QR code on the fridge fixes the half of the problem that was never broken.

The pitch …

ad_detail_evidence.source_text:
Cole Rubin

Promoted by Conduit

Every guidebook, welcome book and QR code on the fridge fixes the half of the problem that was never broken.

The pitch makes sense. Guests have questions, so give them a well-organized place to find the answers. Nicer layout, better categories, a link in the pre-arrival message.

We measured whether any of it lands. In threads where the operator had already sent the door code unprompted, before the guest asked anything, 27.4% of guests asked for it regardless. Check-in time ran 20.8%, wifi 18.4%.

That is information sitting on their phone, in a thread they already have open. If it gets missed there, a PDF will not rescue it.

Most guidebooks are organized fine. The timing is what fails. The information arrives days before anyone wants it, and when they finally do want it, finding it becomes the guest's job.

So we built the other half. Portals is our guest portal, and the AI chat lives in it. The guest asks the question the way they would say it out loud and gets an answer that knows which property they are standing in.

"What's a good dinner spot for us tonight around here."

Keep the guidebook. Just stop expecting it to answer anything.

Link in the comments.

# Conduit: AI agents for hospitality

> An AI agent platform for hospitality. Answer guest messages and calls, handle requests, and coordinate work through your connected PMS and tools.

Conduit serves hotel groups, independent hotels, short-term-rental operators, resorts, aparthotels, and villas. Agents built on Conduit work across email, phone, SMS, WhatsApp, online travel agencies, and connected property-management systems. Conduit is designed for operational work that needs business context, integrations, security controls, observability, and a clear path to a human when automation should stop.

## What Conduit agents do

### Chat agents

Chat agents respond to guest questions across every connected messaging channel. They use property and company knowledge, preserve the operator's tone, coordinate requests, and transfer conversations when a person should take over.

### Voice agents

Voice agents answer calls around the clock for front-desk questions, amenities, restaurants, and group sales. They give hospitality teams a consistent first response without asking staff to monitor every line continuously.

### Internal agents

Internal agents help teams execute multi-step procedures, answer operational questions, and act across connected tools. Conduit includes multilingual support, native integrations, performance reporting, procedure controls, and inspection of the tools and decisions used in each run.

## When to use Conduit

Use Conduit when a hospitality business needs to handle repetitive guest communication, provide reliable after-hours coverage, coordinate work across properties, or automate a documented internal procedure. It is best suited to teams that want agents connected to their property-management and operating systems with enterprise security and measurable performance. Keep human approval and escalation in the loop for sensitive, exceptional, or irreversible decisions.

# AI agents for handling guest operations end to end

> Answer messages and calls, retrieve context, and take action in your connected tools. Agents escalate to your team when they’re needed.

## Answer the question. Handle the request.

Give agents your property information, procedures, and access to the tools they need.

### Answer across channels

Handle voice, chat, email, WhatsApp, and connected OTA messages with the guest’s conversation history.

- WhatsApp + SMS
- Email & social
- Voice + chat

### Act on guest requests

Use reservation data and your knowledge base to update bookings, collect payments, and create tasks through connected tools.

- Live PMS
- Knowledge context
- Payments + tasks

### Review and improve replies

Find gaps in agent responses, review proposed fixes, and test changes before guests see them.

- Review outcomes
- Propose fixes
- Backtested

## Results

- Property-specific answers: Agents use your property information and policies to answer guest questions.
- Actions in connected tools: Check bookings, make reservation changes, and create tasks through supported integrations.
- Rules you set: Define the procedures agents follow and the requests your team should handle.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is an AI guest communication agent?

An AI agent answers guest messages and calls using your property information and reservation data. It can also take actions through connected tools, such as creating a task or updating a booking, and pass requests to your team.

### How much can Conduit's agents resolve on their own?

The share depends on your guest requests, knowledge base, integrations, and escalation rules. Track resolved conversations and handoffs to see what your agents can handle and where they need help.

### Do Conduit agents handle phone calls as well as messaging?

Yes. Conduit supports phone calls as well as chat, email, WhatsApp, and connected OTA messages. Agents use your property information and escalation rules across those channels.

### How do the agents know my property's policies?

You provide policies and property details in a configurable knowledge base. Agents combine that information with reservation data from your connected systems.

A fleet of on-brand agents handles the entire guest journey across every channel, converting inquiries into bookings, driving upsell revenue, running internal operations, and surfacing insights for leadership, all connected to the systems operators already use.

Guests can’t buy what they don’t see.

If your upsells sit on a page guests never open, even the right offer can go unnoticed.

A conversation gives you another way to surface it.

A guest asks about dinner. Your AI recommends your private-chef experience and answers their questions.

Another mentions arriving before check-in. Your AI offers early check-in, when it’s available.

Neither guest needs to know what you sell or ask for it by name. The recommendation starts with what they need.

The conversation introduces a relevant offer. The portal lets guests explore the details, browse other upsells, and instantly pay with Apple or Google Pay.

Guests ask the same things, in the same order, every single stay.

We compiled a breakdown of message topics of over 10 million guest messages across 120+ countries.

Our team mapped each stay into topic buckets shown below:

𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸-𝗶𝗻
- 8+ days out: Booking and property questions 
- 1-7 days out: Verification and early check-in

𝗗𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆
- On check-in day: Access and entry, right at check-in and throughout
- Throughout: Appliance and amenity questions/requests

𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸-𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗼𝘀𝘁-𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆
- During check-out: Departure logistics peak
- Post check-out: Payments and (unfortunately) complaints

How can you use make use of this data? 

𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸-𝗶𝗻.
It's between 5-9% of every pre-arrival conversation. If you're answering it that often, it's a product you can price as an upsell. Better yet, offer it in a portal that they can see while going through check-in steps.

𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗹𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲.
Verification 10%, early check-in 9%, arrival logistics 11%. Sending a portal for ID collection, early check-in requests, and directions that link to Maps removes about 30% of conversation volume. Guests prefer that anyway!

𝗦𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸-𝗶𝗻 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘆.
If guests are self-checking-in, send a quick message after the scheduled time. A simple "did you get in ok?" around 30 minutes to an hour after check-in improves guest review scores and gets ahead of any issues.

𝗦𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗮 𝗺𝗶𝗱-𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸-𝗶𝗻.
Hear out guests while you can still improve the stay - complaints are 4% during the stay and 9% after checkout. After check-out, the reviews are already written and all you can do is refund.

𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸-𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘆
Offer a priced or complimentary late check-out. Every guest appreciates it.

A trick we reserve for Conduit customers is an agent that generates a personalized follow-up - around the one-month post check-out. We've seen direct-booking conversations go up about 30% as a result of that one message.

All of this runs on Conduit today. Book a demo in the comments below.

AI Concierge

After-Hours Receptionist
Conduit's voice agents answer inbound calls 24/7 with full PMS context, so guests reach an AI receptionist who already knows their name, booking, and property details before the conversation starts.
Always-On Front Desk
Guest questions, maintenance requests, housekeeping coordination, access codes — Conduit's AI agent handles the high-volume communication that currently lands at your desk, so your team focuses on the 20% that genuinely needs them.
Operations
Daily Ops Brief
Describe what you want to see each morning in plain language. Conduit reads your PMS, your ops board, and your guest conversations overnight, and the brief is waiting in your inbox, Slack, or WhatsApp when you sit down.
Housekeeping Board
Room status, section assignments, and the daily sheet stay live against your PMS. When a guest asks for a late checkout or a room turns dirty, the board updates itself and the affected team hears about it.
Maintenance & Work Orders
A guest reports a problem and the work order opens itself: vendor assigned, access code issued, room status changed, guest updated. Your engineer finds out from the task, not from the front desk.
Review Signals
Breakfast mentioned negatively nine times this month is not a review problem, it is an F&B problem. Conduit groups feedback by theme, sends it to the department that owns it, and opens the task.
Supplies & Par Levels
Par levels that account for next week's occupancy, not last month's average. When stock drops below par, the agent raises the order against your approved supplier and tells you what it costs.

Guest Experience
No app required. No portal to navigate. Guests text from their personal messaging app, call from their phone, or reach out via WhatsApp — and your AI agent handles every request in the channels they already use.
Guest Feedback
Post-stay surveys measure the experience. Conduit shapes it while the guest is still on property — acknowledging issues, dispatching resolutions, and sending follow-up requests through the channel the guest is already using.
Guest Memory (CRM)
Traditional platforms pull booking history and spend data from your PMS. Conduit captures the preferences guests mention in WhatsApp messages, the upgrade they accepted, and the complaint that revealed a service gap — and surfaces them on the next stay.
Review Responses
Traditional review platforms respond after the review is published. Conduit works upstream — resolving complaints before checkout and drafting responses with the full conversation thread from that guest's stay.

Room Upgrades

The Challenge
Haven Vacation Rentals manages roughly 270 short-term rental properties across Tennessee's Smoky Mountains. At its peak, the company had around 25 people in guest support, split across morning, evening, and weekend shifts. Five or six per shift, fielding every check-in question, lockout, cleaning issue, and complaint that came through.
Jack, Haven's CEO, watched the volume climb with every property added. Growth meant more messages, more calls, and more staff. The economics worked, but the model didn't scale without proportional headcount.
Haven had Conduit installed but was barely using it. Listings were uploaded, general information was filled in, and the system ran at about 40 percent automation with no workflows and minimal knowledge base work. Enough to take the edge off, not enough to change how the team operated.
Jack and his partner looked at the year ahead and realized they couldn't keep up at the current pace.
"We had a really big year in 2025, so I was like, I can't do this," Jack said. "And my partner was like, we're not gonna be able to do this ourselves."
The Solution
Haven's approach started with the team, not the technology.
Jack gathered the support staff for a meeting. He drew a hard line: their jobs were safe, and the goal was to make the AI as good as possible.
"I made a very hard line in the sand," Jack said. "Your new job is gonna get as good as this as possible. We're not gonna lay anyone off. That's not happening."
The first meeting didn't land. The team didn't believe him. He held two more before people started to buy in.
Once they had trust, Jack tied a incentives to the automation rate. Jonathan, the guest services manager, became the central person teaching the AI. Having one source of truth mattered because different team members handled the same situations in different ways. A door lock issue at 8 AM got a different response than one at 4 PM. Jonathan standardized those answers.
The team created a Slack channel called AI Avengers. Anytime the AI handled something poorly, people posted screenshots. Jonathan and Jack would respond with guidance on whether to teach the AI or adjust a workflow.
The push from 40 to 80 percent automation took a couple of months. Getting from 80 to 90 required more creative problem-solving, but Haven held quality scores at 4.8 or 4.9 the entire time. The incentive was tied to both metrics: automation rate had to climb, and scores couldn't drop.
The Transformation
At 90 percent automation, Haven's support workload inverted. The AI handled routine guest communication across 270 properties. The team focused on guests with real problems.
Jack saw it during a snowstorm. Ninety guests checked in the same day the Smokies got eight inches of snow. People were stuck. They couldn't get in or out. The automation rate held steady, and only three issues needed a human.
"This happened before," Jack said. "I remember looking at my phone, and I'm like, how in the world am I gonna look at all 100 of these problems? Then on Sunday, I looked, and there was three things. And I was like, oh, this is great. We can solve three."
The team that used to copy-paste door codes now builds workflows and trains the AI. Jack gives them problems to solve. One recent example: every time a guest brings a dog to a specific set of properties, the system needs to notify the cleaning company and push the information back. Jonathan built the workflow in about an hour, figuring it out through trial and error.
"That's how we've trained," Jack said. "Give them these problems. They just went and built the workflow and figured it out."
Haven also rethought how the AI communicates during gaps in its knowledge. Instead of stalling or guessing, the AI tells the guest it needs a moment to check with the team and will follow up within two or three minutes. Then it runs the workflow. Jack credits that small change with building guest trust, even when the AI doesn't have an immediate answer.
The staffing math changed permanently. Haven went from needing around 25 support staff to running with two people per shift. Nobody was laid off because of the AI. Some left for other reasons. Others moved into different roles. As more listings come on, Jack pulls people further into conversational engineering rather than hiring new support reps.
"We added 14 listings in January," Jack said. "We haven't had to add anyone."
Results
90 percent automation rate
across 270 properties, up from 40 percent
80 percent reduction in support staffing needs
—from 25 people to two per shift
59 percent of listings
earned Airbnb Guest Favorite status
14 listings added in January
without hiring additional support staff
Maintained super host and premier host status
throughout the automation push
Team members transitioned from reactive support to
workflow building and AI training
Looking Ahead
Haven is rebuilding its Slack triage workflows and expanding how the team uses Conduit's workflow engine. Jack is also exploring homeowner acquisition workflows with voice AI for inbound phone leads.
The knowledge base work continues. Jack's advice: don't try to finish it in two weeks.
"You can get automation quickly, but I think where people make a mistake is, the next two weeks, we're just grinding on this, and we're gonna be done," Jack said. "Do a two-week sprint, but if you really kinda just pick away at it for six months and just think, hey, we don't need to rush into anything, I think over time, it's just good to teach it and go on."

USING CONDUIT SINCE:
December 2024
"The more hands-off the property, the higher the valuation. We choose Conduit for that."
Noel Poler
Founder, The Lauderdale Boutique Hotel
A hotel that ran itself. No fires to put out. No Slack threads to monitor. Guest support was handled—and guests were happy. That was the point.
Hotel owner Noel Poler has a theory: better systems elevate not just service but valuation of the hotel, the underlying asset itself. With Conduit, he put theory to practice. By replacing a traditional call center with Conduit’s AI-powered support platform and 24/7 staffed support team, Noel and The Lauderdale Boutique Hotel improved margins, reduced disputes, and turned it into a passive investment operational model. The result? A hotel with better reviews, faster support, and more than $500,000 gain in real estate value.
The Challenge
Noel had run through multiple support models—first Jurny’s PMS and call center, then other hospitality-focused call services. Costs started at $4,000, and even though he was able bring them down to $1,200 a month, service was inconsistent. Guests were waiting up to an hour for replies. Noel was still answering questions himself in Slack. Refunds were mounting. Response delays and miscommunications chipped away at both guest experience and profits.
"Living on Slack is not the definition of a passive investment," Noel said.
He wanted something sustainable: a way to make the property truly hands-off for and investor, while delivering excellent service and peace of mind.
The Solution: Automation That Adds to the NOI and Turns it into a Passive Investment
Switching to Conduit brought three key changes: speed, savings, and a lot less work (turning it into a passive investment!). Guest response time dropped from 57 minutes to 2 minutes on average, and instant responses to the vast majority of issues. Guest satisfaction increased and therefore refunds decreased. And support costs dropped to just $600 per month—a fraction of what he used to pay.
Key results from using Conduit:
Reduced support costs from $4,000 to $600/month
Increased NOI by at least $3,400/month through reduced costs, and significant fewer refunds
Improved average response time from 57 minutes to 2 minutes on average, and instantaneous responses for most issues.
Enabled part-time property manager to efficiently oversee property
Highlighted tech stack with Conduit as key pilar as part of asset value in Offering Memorandum
"We tell investors, this isn’t just tech for convenience. It’s real leverage." Noel said.
At an 8% Cap Rate, that $3,400 monthly gain translates into over $500,000 in added asset value. Turning it into a passive investment lowers the Cap Rate at which it will sell, at 7% Cap Rate those $3,400 monthly savings turn into almost $600,000
The Impact
Noel had long believed tech centric operations would yield long-term value. Conduit validated that belief. With a lean team and AI handling routine communication, he spends a lot less time in the weeds and more time generating value.
"The more hands-off the property, the higher the valuation. We designed and built for that." Noel added.
Conduit also became a differentiator in his sales process. As Noel prepares to bring the property to market, the Offering Memorandum includes a section on operational technology—with Conduit front and center highlighting it as a hands-off passive investment, closer to a traditional multifamily, with the higher rents short term rentals generate.
Looking Ahead
Most boutique hotel owners still run things the old way. But Noel sees a different future. With tools like Conduit, a single manager can oversee multiple properties. And investors can treat hospitality assets more like traditional long term rentals: passive, scalable, and increasingly automated.
"Conduit keeps improving. That’s why I chose them. In a space where tech, and particularly AI, improves daily, I wanted a partner who could keep up" Noel stressed.
Noel isn’t waiting for the industry to catch up. He’s building what comes next and showing the numbers to prove it.

ABOUT:
Locally owned and operated, we offer handpicked vacation rentals across Oregon’s most beautiful destinations.
USING CONDUIT SINCE:
December 2024
“Our long-term mission is that if you're not boots on the property or interacting with a guest, you're AI”
Ryan
Revenue & Guest Services, Cascadia Getaways
The growth bottleneck nobody talks about
Property management companies hit a familiar ceiling. The portfolio grows, but the support team can't keep up. Hiring takes time, and by the time new staff are properly trained and productive, the next growth spurt is already demanding another round of recruiting.
Cascadia Getaways broke that cycle. When the company acquired its first property management business this year, leadership didn't worry about guest services capacity.
"We just bought our first company and integrated it this week," said Ryan, who leads revenue and guest services. "Just knowing we can add another company's worth of properties in and not needing to hire additional guest service staff feels pretty good."
The infrastructure that made it possible
Cascadia Getaways deployed Conduit in March. Within months, the company reached 60 percent automation  and 4.9 communication scores across across 100 properties.
The impact on staffing has been quickly visible.
"We don't have to hire more headcount to pick up the phones," Ryan said. Normally, a company would have to scale their support team significantly to cover busy periods, but not them, instead they even made the role evolved. They're now curating the data added to the knowledge base to ensure the AI has the right information, and also spend more time on high-value tasks like upselling calls before guests arrive.
AI handles routine inquiries like lockbox codes, parking rules, local recommendations, and standard troubleshooting. Humans step in for escalations and anything requiring genuine empathy.
Quality didn't suffer
Efficiency gains often trade against service quality. Cascadia Getaways's numbers show the opposite.
Before Conduit, communication scores fluctuated between 4.8 and 4.9. After deployment, the score locked at 4.9 and hasn't dipped. "We haven't gone below 4.9 in the communication score," Ryan said. Guest reviews cite responsive, knowledgeable support. The AI's ability to pull local recommendations, hiking trails, restaurants, packing lists, creates an impression of on-the-ground expertise. "They really think they're talking to somebody local," Ryan said. "Which is huge."
From reactive to proactive
The team now runs programs that most property managers can't staff because they're too reactive, constantly fielding incoming requests.
Pre-arrival calls
go out before every stay. Team members confirm 24/7 availability, capture travel details, and reinforce brand recognition. Guests who booked through Airbnb learn the management company's name, critical for direct booking conversion later.
Post-stay calls
happen after checkout but before review requests. The timing is intentional. "That post-stay call gives the guests the opportunity to vent a little bit if they have any issues that came up before the review ask comes out," Ryan explained. Team members also mention that booking direct saves 15 to 20 percent.
Concierge calls
arrive two weeks before check-in. The day team offers in-home chefs, massage therapists, and local experience coordination. A vacation rental becomes a hospitality experience.
The AI strategy advantage
Ryan frames automation as competitive positioning: "I haven't met another property manager who has an AI strategy."
Most operators react to AI, experimenting with tools, testing features, seeing what sticks. Cascadia Getaways built a philosophy around it.
"Our long-term mission is that if you're not boots on the property or interacting with a guest, you're AI," Ryan said.
The framing clarifies every decision. Should AI handle this task? Only if it doesn't require physical presence or human connection. Should we hire for this role? Only if the work can't be automated.
The result: resources concentrate on property managers and cleaners, the roles that define guest experience.
"I want to have the highest paid property managers in the market because then we corner the market on talent," Ryan said. "Finding the best cleaners and the best managers is real hard in these markets."
Team evolution
When AI arrived, leadership addressed the obvious fear directly.
"It started off very much like making sure they felt comfortable with the fact that AI wasn't going to take their job," Ryan said. "AI was there so they could work on higher-level projects, more fun things."
The promise held. Team members expanded into new domains. One night-shift employee manages SEO and Google Analytics, and organic traffic has grown. Another night-shift team member is learning revenue management. Day staff run concierge programs and proactive outreach.
"They're not just playing guest service agents," Ryan said. "They're getting involved with more segments of the business because of this automation."
Morale reflects the shift. "It gives them more confidence. They're working for a company that's on the winning side. It always feels good to be a winner."
Documentation as a forcing function
Conduit implementation required Cascadia Getaways to formalize processes. Like many property management companies, Cascadia Getaways had grown organically without developing extensive standard operating procedures. Knowledge about property-specific details, guest communication protocols, and troubleshooting steps lived exclusively in the team's collective experience.
The AI deployment forced documentation. Policies, procedures, and edge cases now live in a knowledge base that trains both the AI and new hires.
"Now we have a manual for running a segment of our business," Ryan said. The documentation supports Cascadia Getaways's longer-term goal: building operational playbooks for the entire company.
What growth looks like now
The integration framework is set. New acquisitions drop into an infrastructure built to absorb them, without proportional headcount increases, without service degradation, without the traditional scramble.
"It's really allowed us to grow with confidence," Ryan said.
The next frontier: expanding Conduit beyond guest communications. Ryan envisions a unified platform handling homeowner inquiries, vendor coordination, and cleaner communication.
"I would love to have Conduit just be the control panel for everyone externally that we need to communicate with."
Results:
60 percent automation rate
150 properties per support rep on shift
4.9 communication score (maintained post-deployment)
Team members upskilled into SEO, revenue management, and concierge services
